*Why this is the best choice:*  
- **...Rb4+** delivers an immediate check, forcing White’s king to move (only Ka5 or Ka3 are legal).  
- The rook now occupies the critical fourth rank, cutting off the a‑file and preparing for follow‑up checks that will drive the white king toward the edge of the board.  
- With the additional support of the pawn on c5 and the knight on g5, Black can continue with precise checking moves (e.g., Ra4+, Nd2!, c4!) to restrict the king’s escape squares and eventually force a forced mate in a few more turns.  

All other legal moves either do not give check or allow White to escape or defend more easily. Therefore **b8b4** is the decisive, forcing move that leads to a winning position for Black.

Player_Black (to Proxy):



**c2b4**  

The knight on c2 can jump to b4, giving check to the white king on a2.  
After this move the black queen still controls the entire first rank (a1‑h1), so any attempt by White to escape on b1 or a1 is impossible because those squares are under attack by the queen.  

The only square left for the white king after 1…Nb4+ is **a3** (the other two squares, b2 and b3, are also covered by the queen’s diagonal from c3).  
From there Black follows up with **Qc3#**:

* 1…Nb4+ Ka3  
* 2.Qc3#  

All adjacent escape squares are either occupied by friendly pieces or are attacked by Black (the knight on b4 attacks a2 and a4; the queen on c3 attacks b2, b3 and a3). No White piece can interpose or capture the checking pieces, so it is checkmate.

If White tries to avoid the mate by moving the king elsewhere (e.g., Kb2 or Kb3), Black still has a forced sequence leading to mate in one more move (for example 1…Nb4+ Kb2 Qa5+ Ka3 Qa2#). In every line Black delivers checkmate on the second move, so **c2b4** is the decisive winning move.
